rewritten_text:
Even reading about the splendour enjoyed by the dead was marvellous.

Next he became interested in embroidery and the tapestries that served in place of frescoes in the cold rooms of northern Europe. As he explored the subject—he had an exceptional ability to immerse himself completely, for the moment, in whatever attracted him—he felt almost sad at the thought of time destroying such beautiful, extraordinary things. He, at least, had escaped that fate. Summer succeeded summer; the yellow jonquils blossomed and withered over and over; nights of horror repeated their shameful story. Yet he remained the same. No winter damaged his face or dulled its flowerlike freshness. How differently physical objects fared! Where had they all gone? Where was the magnificent crocus-coloured robe, embroidered by brown-skinned girls for Athena’s pleasure, showing the gods battling the giants? Where was the enormous awning Nero had spread above the Colosseum in Rome, that titanic purple sail depicting a star-filled sky and Apollo driving a chariot pulled by white horses with gilded reins? He yearned to see the remarkable table napkins made for the Priest of the Sun, displaying every delicacy and dish that a banquet might require; King Chilperic’s burial cloth with its three hundred golden bees; the extravagant robes that had outraged the Bishop of Pontus, decorated with lions, panthers, bears, dogs, forests, rocks, hunters—everything, in fact, that an artist could reproduce from nature. He wanted to see the coat once worn by Charles of Orleans, its sleeves embroidered with the verses of a song beginning ‘Madame, je suis tout joyeux.’ The music accompanying the words was stitched in gold thread, each note—square in those days—made from four pearls. He read about the room prepared for Queen Joan of Burgundy at the palace in Rheims: thirteen hundred and twenty-one embroidered parrots bearing the king’s coat of arms, and five hundred and sixty-one butterflies whose wings bore the queen’s arms, all worked in gold. Catherine de Medicis had commissioned a mourning bed of black velvet scattered with crescents and suns. Its damask curtains displayed leafy wreaths and garlands against a background of gold and silver, with pearl embroidery fringing their edges. The bed stood in a room hung with silver cloth bearing rows of the queen’s emblems in cut black velvet. In Louis XIV’s apartment stood images of caryatides, female figures serving as columns, embroidered in gold and fifteen feet high.

‘Not everyone would have been so kind and determined, refusing to take no for an answer from Jane. But yesterday she said firmly that she would not write to turn down the offer, as Jane had asked. She would wait. And sure enough, that evening it was decided that Jane would go! I was completely surprised. I hadn’t the slightest idea! Jane took Mrs. Elton aside and told her that she had thought about the advantages of working for Mrs. Smallridge and had decided to accept the job. I heard nothing about it until everything was settled.’

‘You were with Mrs. Elton last night?’

‘Yes, all of us. She insisted on our coming. It was arranged up on the hill, while we were walking around with Mr. Knightley. “You must all come to us this evening,” she said. “I absolutely must have you all.”’

‘And Mr. Knightley went too?’

‘No, not Mr. Knightley. He refused the invitation from the beginning. I thought he might come after all, because Mrs. Elton said she wouldn’t let him escape, but he didn’t. My mother and Jane and I were there, and we had a lovely evening. With such kind friends, Miss Woodhouse, one must always enjoy oneself. Everyone did seem rather worn out after the morning’s party, though. Even having fun is tiring, you know, and I can’t say any of them seemed to have enjoyed the outing very much. But I shall always think of it as a pleasant party, and feel very grateful to the kind friends who included me.’

‘I suppose Miss Fairfax was thinking about her decision all day, although you didn’t know it?’

‘I imagine she was.’

‘Whenever she leaves, it must be painful for her and all her friends. But I hope the family’s character and manners will do everything possible to make the job easier for her.’

‘Thank you, dear Miss Woodhouse. Yes, she will have everything she could need to be happy. Except for the Sucklings and the Bragges, none of Mrs. Elton’s friends provides such a generous, elegant setting for raising children. Mrs. Smallridge is a delightful woman! They live almost as grandly as the people at Maple Grove. And the children! Apart from the little Sucklings and Bragges, there are no sweeter or more well-mannered children anywhere. They will treat Jane with such kindness and respect! Her whole life will be nothing but pleasure. And her pay! I really don’t dare tell you how much she’ll earn, Miss Woodhouse.’

Simply reading about the luxurious lives of people long dead filled him with wonder.

He next began studying embroidery and the tapestries that took the place of wall paintings in the cold rooms of northern Europe. Whenever he took up a subject, he had a remarkable gift for losing himself entirely in it. Now, as he studied, he felt almost sad to think how time destroyed things of such beauty and wonder. At least he himself had escaped that destruction. Summer came after summer, the yellow jonquils bloomed and died again and again, and terrible nights repeated their tale of shame. Yet he never changed. No winter spoiled his face or faded its fresh, flowerlike beauty. How different the fate of objects was! Where had they gone? What had become of the great crocus-coloured robe that brown-skinned girls embroidered to please Athena, showing gods fighting giants? Where was the vast covering Nero had stretched over the Colosseum in Rome, a gigantic purple sail decorated with stars and Apollo in a chariot pulled by white horses with gold-covered reins? He longed to see the unusual napkins made for the Priest of the Sun, pictured with all the fine foods anyone could want at a feast. He wished to see King Chilperic’s burial cloth and its three hundred golden bees, and the strange robes that had angered the Bishop of Pontus. Those robes showed lions, panthers, bears, dogs, forests, rocks, and hunters—everything an artist could copy from nature. Then there was the coat Charles of Orleans had worn. A song beginning ‘Madame, je suis tout joyeux’ was embroidered on its sleeves. Its music was sewn in gold thread, and every note, written square in those days, consisted of four pearls. He read about the room arranged for Queen Joan of Burgundy in the palace at Rheims. It held thirteen hundred and twenty-one embroidered parrots decorated with the king’s coat of arms, and five hundred and sixty-one butterflies with the queen’s coat of arms on their wings, all stitched in gold. Catherine de Medicis had ordered a mourning bed of black velvet dotted with crescent moons and suns. Its damask curtains showed leafy wreaths and garlands on a gold and silver background, edged with embroidered pearls. The room around it was hung with silver cloth, covered in rows of the queen’s emblems cut from black velvet. Louis XIV had fifteen-foot images of caryatides—women shaped as supporting columns—embroidered in gold in his apartment.
